Copper Smelter Strike Disrupts Zambia’s Metals & Mining Industry

A major walkout by workers in Zambia’s metals and mining sector entered its third day on Thursday, halting operations at several key copper processing facilities and threatening to slow national production. The industrial action, which began on Tuesday, has directly affected Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd and at least two other major plants in the Copperbelt province.

Union leaders say the strike was called after protracted wage negotiations with mining companies broke down last week. Workers are demanding a 15% pay increase and improved safety measures, citing the rising cost of living and recent workplace incidents.

“The workers have shown unity and resolve,” said Peter Mulenga, spokesperson for the National Mineworkers’ Union of Zambia. “Management must come to the table with a fair offer. Until then, we will remain off the job.”

At Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd, production lines have ground to a halt, with only skeleton staff maintaining essential equipment. Plant manager Joseph Mwansa confirmed that the facility is operating at less than 20% capacity. “We are closely monitoring furnace temperatures and safety systems, but copper output has essentially stopped,” Mwansa said.

Industry analysts warn that the continued strike could have significant repercussions for Zambia’s copper exports. According to the Zambia Metals & Mining Chamber, the walkout is costing the sector an estimated $2.5 million per day in lost output.

“Copper is a lifeline for the national economy, and any prolonged disruption will be deeply felt,” said analyst Linda Chama. “It’s in everyone’s interest to resolve this dispute quickly.”

Negotiations are set to resume on Friday, but so far neither side has indicated a willingness to compromise. Union officials have urged members to remain steadfast, while company leaders stress the need for a sustainable agreement.

Local residents in the mining towns are watching the situation closely. “Many of us depend on these jobs,” said Chambishi resident Grace Banda. “We hope the companies and unions can find common ground soon.”

As the strike continues, all eyes remain on the bargaining table, with the future of the country’s vital metals and mining industry hanging in the balance.
